Project 1¶

Kamran Oskouie¶

For this project I decided to do something I can use in an upcoming interview I have with Intuitive Machines, a lunar lander company. I will be interviewing for a data analyst intern role, so I figured it would be nice if I could describe a real experience working with lunar data. So, for this project, I will be using the Robbins (2018) lunar crater database, about 1.3 million craters, downloaded from USGS as a PDS4 bundle. I will use it to train a model that can predict the density of craters on the Moon based on a set of latitude and longitude coordinates. I will be using k-nearest-neighbor machine learning to achieve this, with 5-fold cross-validation.

I would also like to preface this by saying I have experience with using Python for astronomical research. The beginning of this project will be a lot of manipulating the data and building a spacial distribution, but the second half will be where the machine learning comes in.

The figure below shows the spacial distribution of craters on the Moon. You can see clearly where the maria are, the areas that are more sparsely populated by craters. These are locations that have been essencially repaved with magma, which creates a smoother surface than the rough terrain around it. These are prime locations for landers as there less chance for landing on a ridge or boulder. It should be noted that this is rectangular and the Moon is a sphere, so where it looks less dense on the top and bottom is actually because the distances have been spread out to compensate.

I just wanted to see what this data looks like. Pretty cool, huh?

(180, 90)

Here is where things get tricky. On a sphere, lines of latutude are parallel, however the lines of longitude are not. They are parallel at the equator and intersect at the poles. Since crater density depends on area, we first need to define what area means in the context of the surface of a sphere. The formula below is area of a $2^\circ \times 2^\circ$ patch as a function of latidude. As you get closer to the poles the area approaches 0.

$A = R^2 \Delta \lambda \left( \sin{\phi}_2 - \sin{\phi_1}\right)$

where $R = 1737.4$ km, $\Delta \lambda = 2^\circ = \frac{\pi}{90}$, and $\phi =$ latitude in radians.

In [10]:
R = 1737.4
lam = np.radians(2)
lat_rad = np.radians(lat_edge)
Areas = []
for i in range(90):
    A = R**2 * lam * (np.sin(lat_rad[i+1]) - np.sin(lat_rad[i]))
    Areas.append(A)
Areas[45]
Out[10]:
np.float64(3677.275442840315)
In [11]:
density = counts / np.array(Areas) # divides each latitude column of counts by that band's area to get craters per square km

Below is a visualization of the crater density for each 2 degree square patch of the Moon. the lighter colors represent higher crater density, while the darker color represents lower density. You can see that this map closely resembles the figure from earlier.

Now, to start modeling, the square patches need one set of coordinates each. Below finds the centers of each square and creates two lists for longitude and latitude.

In [13]:
lon = []
for i in range(180):
    center = (lon_edge[i] + lon_edge[i+1]) / 2
    lon.append(center)

lat = []
for i in range(90):
    center = (lat_edge[i] + lat_edge[i+1]) / 2
    lat.append(center)

The goal is to predict density as a function of coordinates, so I created a dictionary for every longitude and latitude, and converted that into a dataframe

In [15]:
lon_col = []
lat_col = []
dens_col = []

for i in range(180):
    for j in range(90):
        lon_col.append(lon[i])
        lat_col.append(lat[j])
        dens_col.append(density[i, j])

patches = pd.DataFrame({'lon': lon_col, 'lat': lat_col, 'density': dens_col})

In class, we have done knn with one input and one output. In this case, our 'one input' is a set of coordinates: longitude and latitude. Luckily scikit-learn handles this easily.

In [17]:
X = patches[['lon','lat']] 
y = patches['density']
In [18]:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor # knn
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_validate, KFold # k-folds
In [19]:
folds = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) # I will be doing 5 folds, with the data randomly shuffled.
# 42 is a convention. I found out this is because of the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy

The code block below loops through values of k from 1 to 100. For each k, it splits the data into 5 folds: 4 become training data and 1 becomes test data. For each patch in the test fold, it predicts the density by averaging its k nearest neighbors from the training data, then calculates the RMSE against the true densities. It repeats this so each fold gets a turn as the test set, averages the 5 RMSEs, and saves that to a list. It does the same for the training error, so I can compare the two.

In [20]:
kvec = range(1, 101) # different values of k, ranging from 1 to 100
train_rmse = [] # this is where the train data errors will go
cv_rmse = [] # this is where the test data errors will go

for k in kvec:
    model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=k)
    results = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=folds, scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error', return_train_score=True)
    cv_rmse.append(-results['test_score'].mean())
    train_rmse.append(-results['train_score'].mean())
In [21]:
# this figure shows the RMSE for each value of k, and compares the test and train data
plt.plot(kvec,cv_rmse, label='test')
plt.plot(kvec,train_rmse, label='train')
plt.xlabel('k')
plt.ylabel('error')
plt.legend()

The figure below shows the density distribution as modeled by k=6. It looks very similar to the original version, just a little more blurry. This makes sense, because ecah patch is the average of it's 6 nearest patches. Super cool!

The next two figures show the 'bias-variance tradeoff'. k=1 is the highest complexity model, and it is a 1 to 1 replica of the original density distribution. k=100 is a low complexity model. It still looks somewhat like the original, but it has a very low variance, and just looks like a super blurry version of the original.

Something I thought about while I was finishing this project: there really isn't much purpose to doing this other than practice. Machine learning is used to make predictions, and my model doesn't really do that. What I mean by that is, if you took my model to Mercury or Mars, is would be absolutely meaningless. So, while it does work for the sake of this project, it doesn't work for the sake of making future predictions. I am still very proud of my work, though, and I think this will make a great story in my upcoming interview :)

One last thing I would like to add to my reflection: this model is actually not very meaningful along the edges of the map. The surface of a sphere is continuous, which would mean the patches along the sides of this map, and particularily close to the poles, should be treated as such. I think, for the scope of this project, what I've done is fine. However, if I were to be more rigorous about this process, I would make sure the map is continuous.

Data Reference¶

Robbins, S. J. (2019). A new global database of lunar impact craters >1–2 km: 1. Crater locations and sizes, comparisons with published databases, and global analysis. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 124, 871–892. https://doi.org/10.1029/2018JE005592

Data downloaded as a PDS4 bundle from the USGS Astrogeology Science Center.
